title: Lucy's Flyby Reveals a Tumbling, Peanut-Shaped Asteroid with a Watery Past
summary: When NASA's Lucy spacecraft buzzed past asteroid Donaldjohanson in April 2025, it expected a routine test. Instead, it found a cosmic oddball: a wobbling, peanut-shaped rock with signs of ancient water. The findings, published in Science on June 18, rewrite what we know about small asteroids. Donaldjohanson is a bilobate asteroid — two lobes connected by a narrow neck, like a peanut. It formed about 155 million years ago when fragments from a violent collision coalesced under their own gravity. But its rotation is anything but simple. Instead of spinning around a single axis, it tumbles end-over-end every 10.5 days while rocking back and forth every 26.5 days. "It behaves more like a wobbling spinning top," researchers noted. What caused this chaotic dance? The YORP effect — a subtle force driven by sunlight. As the asteroid absorbs and re-emits solar radiation, tiny torques act on its irregular shape. Over 20 to 60 million years, this slowed its spin from at least ten times faster, reshaping its surface as loose debris slid down slopes. Lucy's instruments also detected iron-rich clay minerals, clear evidence that liquid water once interacted with the rock. This makes Donaldjohanson a rare window into the hydrated past of asteroids. The flyby, at a distance of just 650 miles, served as a dress rehearsal for Lucy's primary mission: exploring Jupiter's Trojan asteroids, starting with Eurybates in 2027. By comparing Donaldjohanson to previously visited asteroids like Bennu and Ryugu, scientists hope to understand how these ancient bodies evolve. The mission underscores that even small, seemingly simple asteroids can harbor complex, surprising histories — and that sunlight can sculpt worlds in ways we're only beginning to grasp.
why_it_matters: Asteroids aren't just boring rocks — they hold clues to how our solar system formed and how water reached Earth. Studying their wild spins and ancient minerals could one day help us protect our planet from a future impact or unlock the secrets of life's origins.

background_read: The Lucy spacecraft, launched by NASA in 2021, is named after the famous fossil skeleton of an early human ancestor, symbolizing its mission to uncover clues about the solar system's 'infancy.' Its main targets are the Trojan asteroids — two enormous swarms of space rocks that circle the Sun in the same orbit as Jupiter, more than 500 million miles away.

Trojan asteroids are 4.6-billion-year-old time capsules from the birth of the planets. Scientists think some of them may contain water-rich minerals, making them crucial for understanding how water — a key ingredient for life — arrived on Earth.

Donaldjohanson is a much smaller, nearer space rock in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. When Lucy swung by it at just 650 miles (1,050 km) distance, it was a test run for the more ambitious encounters to come, but the data it returned turned out to be scientifically important on its own.

Other recent asteroid missions, like Japan’s Hayabusa2 to Ryugu and NASA’s OSIRIS-REx to Bennu, have collected actual samples and returned them to Earth. Comparing Donaldjohanson’s water-altered minerals to those samples may help piece together a bigger picture of how asteroids change over time.

perspectives.description: Donaldjohanson offers a rare, close-up look at a tumbling asteroid with a watery past. Its iron-rich clays connect it to a class of water-bearing space rocks that may have seeded Earth with oceans, making each new observation a piece of a cosmic puzzle.

The flyby was brief — just a quick snapshot — so some details may remain uncertain. The YORP effect is still not fully understood, and scientists rely on models that might not capture all the complexities of how sunlight reshapes a rock over millions of years.

The asteroid's peanut shape and tumbling motion challenge simple models of rotation. Understanding how irregular bodies respond to solar radiation helps refine physics that applies to everything from space debris to planetary defense — a real-world testbed for orbital mechanics.

Lucy's next targets, the Trojan asteroids, are even more primitive. Comparing this rehearsal data with the Trojans may show how much asteroids change over time. This knowledge could guide future mining missions or inform strategies to deflect a hazardous asteroid heading toward Earth.
